tldr: A data-driven framework to estimate the amount of computation performed by a dynamic system, applied to neural activity in the brain.
motivation: Quantifying computation in real-world systems like the brain is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to physical processes, but existing measures are often abstract or not data-driven.
method: The authors propose a framework based on population neural activity data, using information-theoretic measures to estimate the computational capacity and actual computation performed.
result: The framework provides estimates of computation in neural systems, demonstrating its applicability to experimental data.
conclusion: The approach offers a practical way to measure computation in complex systems, with potential implications for understanding brain function and designing neuromorphic computing.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise using temporal coarse-graining and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with noise exhibiting temporal correlations over many time scales (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging.
method: The noise is expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes; temporal coarse-graining conditions the process on a coarse realization, separating deterministic and bridge components, with ensemble averaging over bridges.
result: The deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and bridge processes are independent with analytically known correlators, enabling precomputation of noise propagators.
conclusion: The approach offers practical advantages like a simple concatenation rule and is demonstrated with numerical examples.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether wide quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation of the circuit.
result: The algorithm computes the NTK and expected output of wide trained QNNs in polynomial time, proving that such networks are classically simulable.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks with Clifford+Pauli structure do not offer quantum advantage, as their training can be efficiently classically simulated.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects that limit acceleration of relaxation in stochastic systems with many degrees of freedom.
method: Experimental optical monitoring of field-induced birefringence combined with Smoluchowski equation modeling; polydispersity generates a spectrum of diffusion coefficients leading to multiscale relaxation.
result: Kovacs nonmonotonic relaxation is observed and explained by polydispersity; sequential suppression of slow modes reduces relaxation time significantly.
conclusion: Memory effects in multiscale stochastic dynamics can be mitigated by mode-suppression protocols, providing a strategy for controlling relaxation in complex systems.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and anyon permutations.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a symmetry, which is important for understanding topological phases and dualities.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define two topological invariants: a homomorphism to anyon permutation symmetries and a generalized GNVW index, and shows equivalence to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, with examples including the Kramers-Wannier duality mapping to anyon permutation in toric code.
conclusion: Subalgebra QCAs are classified by anyon permutation and index, and cannot always be extended to full QCAs, mixing nontrivially with translations.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement in lossy atom interferometers using spin-squeezed states, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but losses degrade performance. The authors aim to quantify realistic gains under lossy conditions.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses from velocity selectivity and scattering. One-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated for phase sensitivity.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses, but finite temperature significantly reduces benefits.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic losses, but practical challenges like temperature must be addressed to realize gains.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying the Pauli principle and a variable bosonic part.
result: A benchmark lithium wave function with hundreds of basis functions is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library for optical layout and demonstrates its use for building modular optical systems for trapped-ion quantum computing.
motivation: Complex optical design in AMO experiments is not scalable due to conventional piecewise setup; a modular, code-to-CAD approach is needed.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to automatically place optical elements, and creates modular baseplates for common subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates.
conclusion: The modular approach enables scaling of optical systems for quantum computers and fosters open-source collaborative hardware design.

title: Classical Field Simulation Of Vortex Lattice Melting In A Two-dimensional Fast Rotating Bose Gas
authors: Sálvio J Bereta, Lucas Madeira, Mônica A Caracanhas, Hélène Perrin And Romain Dubessy
abstract: We present a classical field simulation study of the thermal melting of a two-dimensional (2D) vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on the role of finite-size effects on the melting temperature. This work constitutes a numerical continuation of the recent experimental investigation reported in (Sharma 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett.133 143401), which addressed the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a quasi-2D Bose gas. Using the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap, we simulate the finite-temperature equilibrium state and extract vortex configurations from density snapshots. Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified. Our simulations enable a detailed characterization of the crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases through correlation functions quantifying the translational and orientational order and through defect statistics. Finite-size effects are shown to play a crucial role at lower rotation frequencies, affecting the proliferation of lattice defects.
tldr: Classical field simulation of vortex lattice melting in a rotating 2D Bose gas, focusing on finite-size effects and the KTHNY melting scenario.
motivation: To numerically study the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, complementing recent experiments and clarifying the role of finite-size effects.
method: Uses the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation to simulate finite-temperature equilibrium states in a harmonic plus quartic trap, extracting vortex configurations from density snapshots.
result: Observes clear signatures of two-step KTHNY melting (crystalline, hexatic, liquid phases) and finds that finite-size effects significantly affect defect proliferation at lower rotation frequencies.
conclusion: Finite-size effects are crucial for accurately modeling vortex lattice melting, especially at lower rotation frequencies, and the classical field approach captures the essential physics.

title: Direct Derivation Of The Modified Langevin Noise Formalism From The Canonical Quantization Of Macroscopic Electromagnetism
authors: A Ciattoni
abstract: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models the interaction of the quantized electromagnetic field with an arbitrary lossy magneto-dielectric object placed in vacuum using three types of non-interacting bosonic polaritons: scattering, electric, and magnetic. These respectively represent free-space photons scattered by the object, and photons radiated by quantized electric and magnetic dipolar sources embedded within its volume. Recently (Ciattoni 2024 Phys. Rev. A110 013707), this formalism was justified from the canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) (Philbin 2010 New J. Phys.12 123008) in the Heisenberg picture. This was achieved by identifying the polariton operators within the formal solution of the macroscopic Maxwell equations, assuming they obey bosonic commutation relations to retrieve the canonical ones, and showing they diagonalize the CQME Hamiltonian. However, the explicit functional dependence of these polaritons on the underlying canonical field operators remained undetermined. In this paper, we derive the exact analytical expressions for the polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators. Using these mappings, we provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the MLNF from the canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture. Our derivation is structured in three foundational steps: 1) adopting the derived analytical expressions as the constitutive definitions of the polariton operators; 2) mathematically proving that these operators are strictly bosonic as a direct consequence of the canonical commutation relations; and 3) demonstrating that they exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian.
tldr: This paper derives explicit analytical expressions for polariton operators in the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.
motivation: To provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization, clarifying the relationship between polariton operators and canonical field operators.
method: The authors derive exact analytical mappings between polariton operators and canonical field operators, then prove bosonic commutation relations and diagonalization of the Hamiltonian.
result: Explicit functional forms for scattering, electric, and magnetic polariton operators are obtained, and their bosonic nature and Hamiltonian diagonalization are proven.
conclusion: The modified Langevin noise formalism is rigorously derived from canonical quantization, confirming its consistency and providing a solid foundation for modeling quantized electromagnetic fields in lossy media.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper uses DFT of payoff time series to infer network structure from partial observations in evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring hidden network architecture from limited behavioral data is important for detecting covert actors, unobserved brain regions, or latent molecular regulators.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between the aggregated DFT magnitude of a node's payoff time series and its degree, then use a global-slope fit to estimate degrees and a 'suppress-and-measure' intervention to reveal adjacencies.
result: The method accurately recovers network topology on synthetic and empirical networks, outperforming causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines, and provides bounds on unobserved nodes.
conclusion: The DFT-based approach offers a deterministic, scalable route to structure discovery under partial observability.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies how squeezed light affects electron trajectories in strong field ionization, using a classical trajectory Monte Carlo method.
motivation: To understand how quantum statistics of light (squeezing) can modify ultrafast electron dynamics beyond classical field expectations.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte Carlo technique to simulate strong field ionization by squeezed states of light.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum shows rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Tuning quantum statistics of light offers experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics, but atomic potential remains crucial.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which had not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically simulate the propagation of vortex solitons.
result: They find two classes of stable vortex solitons with in-phase or out-of-phase bright spots, and show that low-charge vortex solitons can be stable, with stability intervals broadening as rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on elastic and magnetic coupling.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic orders in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, possibly due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression due to oxide coverage.
motivation: To understand the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices with metal-oxide layers, which is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance.
method: In operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution is used to image the valence band edge across the device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: The electric field in graphene covered with oxides is suppressed by up to 50% compared to bare graphene, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to uncover potential landscapes in 2D devices, enabling advanced device engineering.

title: Random-with-constraints: Constructing Minimal Models For High-dimensional Biology
authors: Ilya Nemenmanpankaj Mehtaahttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Physics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322bhttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Biology, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322chttps://ror.org/03czfpz43initiative In Theory And Modeling Of Living Systems, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322dhttps://ror.org/05qwgg493department Of Physics, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215ehttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing And Data Science, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215

Biologists and physicists have a rich tradition of modeling dynamics of living systems with simple models composed of a few interacting components. Despite the remarkable success of this approach, it remains unclear how to use such finely tuned models to ...
tldr: This paper proposes a method for constructing minimal models of high-dimensional biological systems using random constraints.
motivation: Biologists and physicists often use simple models for complex living systems, but it is unclear how to systematically derive such models from data.
method: The authors introduce a 'random-with-constraints' framework that generates minimal models by imposing random constraints that match observed statistics.
result: The approach yields interpretable models that capture essential features of high-dimensional biological data.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to construct minimal models for complex biological systems, bridging data-driven and theory-driven approaches.

title: Fractional Charge Density Functional Theory Elucidates Electro-inductive And Electric Field Effects At Electrochemical Interfaces
authors: Jun-Hyeong Kimweitao Yangahttps://ror.org/00py81415department Of Chemistry, Duke University, Durham, NC 27708
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
SignificanceApplying voltages to self-assembled monolayers formed on electrodes allows for dynamic tuning of the chemical properties of the immobilized molecules. A theoretical understanding of the role of voltage will benefit the design of chemical ...
tldr: This paper uses fractional charge density functional theory to study electro-inductive and electric field effects at electrochemical interfaces, focusing on voltage-tuned chemical properties of self-assembled monolayers.

abstract: We study real-time photoionization flux at the Amusia–Cooper minimum (ACM) in argon using ab initio simulations with the relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) method in length (LG) and velocity (VG) gauges. A simple analytical model is used to interpret the results, and to construct Wigner delays and Wigner distributions for both gauges and relativistic channels of the photoelectron ( with and ). The two gauges are found to produce qualitatively different ionization dynamics, with LG having positive and VG having negative Wigner delays. The advancement of several femtoseconds, found for Wigner delays in VG, raises some concern for causality when atoms are ionized by attosecond pulses that are shorter than the absolute value of the Wigner delay. Reassuringly, numerical simulations of wave packets with RTDCIS show that the electrons behave in a causal way in both gauges. Weighted delays that take into account the temporal window of excitation (or the bandwidth of the pulses) are constructed from the Wigner distribution to reach agreement between the numerical simulations and our simple wave packet model. Furthermore, a strong effect of spin–orbit coupling of the photoelectron ( ) is reported for ultrafast photoionization dynamics, and Schrödinger kitten and cat states are identified in the Wigner distributions as a result of the ACM. Our work paves the way for a deeper understanding of ultrafast photoionization and the role of causality in systems with strong electron–electron correlation effects.

method: Ab initio simulations using relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) in length and velocity gauges, combined with a simple analytical model.
result: Length gauge yields positive Wigner delays while velocity gauge yields negative delays of several femtoseconds, but numerical wave-packet simulations confirm causal behavior in both gauges.
conclusion: Weighted delays constructed from Wigner distributions reconcile gauge differences, and spin-orbit coupling significantly affects ultrafast dynamics; Schrödinger kitten/cat states emerge at the ACM.

title: Nucleation Of Adamantane Clusters In Weakly Ionised Plasmas: Dispersion Cohesion, Surface Energy, And Charging
authors: Johannes Fiedler And Justas Zalieckas
abstract: The formation of molecular clusters in low-temperature plasmas is governed by an intricate interplay of dispersion interactions, electrostatic charging, and surface energetics. While chemical growth pathways have been extensively studied, the role of non-chemical interactions in determining characteristic cluster sizes remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop a unified free-energy framework for molecular clusters embedded in weakly ionised Ar/H plasmas. The approach combines first-principles calculations of the molecular polarisability of adamantane with a dielectric description of the plasma response, including collisional damping and plasma screening. Dispersion interactions are treated as a bulk-like cohesive contribution with a physically motivated microscopic cutoff, while electrostatic charging is described within floating-potential theory. We show that, for realistic discharge parameters, the total free energy does not generally exhibit an effective equilibrium radius. Instead, the free-energy landscape is characterised by a nucleation barrier with an effective critical radius separating subcritical clusters from downhill growth. By mapping this nucleation threshold scale as a function of pressure, electron temperature, and gas composition, we demonstrate that plasma conditions provide a systematic control over the nucleation scale. Our results suggest that experimentally observed steady cluster sizes in weakly ionised plasmas are governed by kinetic balance rather than free-energy minimisation, and that gas composition and plasma parameters can be used as effective control knobs for early-stage cluster formation.

motivation: To understand the role of non-chemical interactions in determining cluster sizes in low-temperature plasmas, which is poorly understood.
method: Develops a unified free-energy model combining first-principles polarisability calculations with a dielectric plasma description, including collisional damping and screening.
result: The free-energy landscape shows a nucleation barrier with a critical radius; no equilibrium radius exists; cluster sizes are governed by kinetic balance.
conclusion: Plasma conditions (pressure, electron temperature, gas composition) can control nucleation scale, but steady sizes result from kinetics, not free-energy minimization.

title: Photon Accelerator In Magnetized Electron–ion Plasma

abstract: Strong magnetic fields and plasmas are intrinsically linked in both terrestrial laboratory experiments and in space phenomena. One of the most profound consequences of that is the change in relationship between the frequency and the wave number of electromagnetic waves propagating in plasma in the presence of such magnetic fields when compared to the case without these fields. Furthermore, magnetic fields alter electromagnetic wave interaction with relativistic plasma waves, resulting in different outcomes for particle and radiation generation. For a relativistic plasma wave-based photon acceleration this leads to an increased frequency gain and, thus, potentially to higher efficiency. The influence of a magnetic field leads to quantitative and qualitative change in the properties of photon acceleration, amplifying the increase in the electromagnetic wave frequency.

conclusion: Magnetic fields can enhance photon acceleration in plasma, which may have applications in generating high-frequency radiation.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.

result: Identifies a hidden defect extension of 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel double-particle operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in conformal field theories.

title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing
authors: Hanxu Ma, Shunda Qiao, Ying He, Haiyue Sun And Yufei Ma
abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.

result: The sensor achieves excellent linearity for CH4 and C2H2 with low systematic errors (0.54% and 0.79%) and detection limits of 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm respectively.
conclusion: The proposed OPM-LITES sensor provides a simple, efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection with a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling.
